title: A universe without gravitational waves
deck: Remove a dimension, and gravity loses its ripples. The interesting part is what refuses to disappear.
text:
Imagine being told that you can make quantum gravity easier by removing one direction of space. That sounds like a reasonable bargain. Fewer coordinates, fewer components, fewer things to go wrong.

The surprise is that you lose more than a direction. In three spacetime dimensions, vacuum Einstein gravity has no local propagating gravitational waves. There is no little graviton wave packet you can launch across an otherwise empty universe. The usual local dynamical protagonist has left the stage.

It is tempting to close the book here. A theory of gravity with nothing waving: surely this is a very elaborate way of describing nothing?

The rest of this series is about why that conclusion fails.

## A small room tells you very little

In three dimensions, the Riemann curvature tensor is completely determined by the Ricci tensor. Once the vacuum Einstein equations fix the latter, they fix the local curvature. With a negative cosmological constant, every sufficiently small vacuum patch looks like anti-de Sitter space. With zero cosmological constant, it looks flat.

This is a local statement. The word matters. A flat sheet and a cylinder can look identical to an observer who only examines a tiny neighborhood. Walking around the cylinder reveals information that the tiny neighborhood could never supply. Spacetime has more complicated versions of this distinction: identifications, noncontractible loops, and boundaries.

The early work of Deser, Jackiw, and ’t Hooft made the physical importance of global geometry especially concrete through particles and conical defects. A point source can change how a locally flat region fits together around it.[1] The particle example includes matter, of course; it is not a vacuum counterexample. Its purpose is to train the eye. Curvature in the immediate neighborhood is not a complete inventory of the world.

## What survives the subtraction?

Suppose you wanted to tell a friend exactly which universe you had built. “Every small patch has this curvature” would not be enough. You would also need to say how the patches join, which loops can shrink, and what happens at the edge. Even in the absence of matter, those questions survive.

And once there is an edge, another distinction appears. A change that is merely a relabeling in the interior can alter physically meaningful data at the boundary. Removing bulk waves does not automatically remove boundary excitations. We will meet this distinction in the next article, where it becomes an unexpectedly large symmetry algebra.

Witten’s 1988 treatment turned the special structure of three-dimensional gravity into a concrete quantization program.[2] But “a tractable formulation” and “a uniquely specified quantum theory answering every gravitational question” are different achievements. Boundaries and the allowed global configurations still need to be chosen.

## Why this is a good place to get confused

Three-dimensional gravity is useful because several questions that are tangled together in higher dimensions can be pulled apart. Which difficulty came from local waves? Which came from topology? Which came from summing over geometries? Which came from deciding what a boundary observer is allowed to measure?

That is also why calling it a toy model can be misleading. A toy is useful when removing details makes the mechanism visible. Here the mechanism that becomes visible is how much of gravity was never about local waves in the first place.

One qualification will stay with us: throughout this route, “no local gravitons” refers to ordinary vacuum Einstein gravity. Add suitable higher-derivative terms or matter and the story changes. We have chosen a particular laboratory, not established a theorem about everything called gravity in three dimensions.

For now, keep the room small and the questions large. The room looks simple. What happens at its boundary does not.

refs: Brown & Henneaux (1986), Central Charges in the Canonical Realization of Asymptotic Symmetries
Strominger (1997/1998), Black Hole Entropy from Near-Horizon Microstates
title: The edge has more to say
deck: A transformation can be empty bookkeeping in the bulk and a physical operation at infinity.
text:
If a theory has no local gravitational waves, where could its states hide? One answer begins with an apparently dull task: specify what the metric is allowed to do far away.

Boundary conditions sound like the fine print beneath the physics. In anti-de Sitter gravity, they are part of the physics. They tell us what we hold fixed, which variations belong to the same problem, and which transformations can carry a charge.

The edge is not simply where the calculation stops. It helps decide what the calculation means.

## A change of coordinates, with consequences

General relativity teaches us to be suspicious of coordinates. Two metrics related by a harmless change of labels should not be counted as two universes. But “harmless” depends on what happens at the boundary.

Think of moving every object in a room together with the ruler used to locate them. That changes no relative measurement. Now imagine the ruler is attached to a wall that the experiment holds fixed. A transformation that acts on the wall needs a different assessment. This is only an analogy, but it points toward the distinction between gauge redundancies with vanishing charges and asymptotic symmetries with nonzero charges.

Brown and Henneaux examined asymptotically AdS₃ metrics under specific boundary conditions in 1986. The resulting symmetry was much larger than the finite-dimensional isometry group of exact AdS₃: the charge algebra contains two Virasoro algebras.[1] The boundary supports an infinite family of transformations.

There is an especially memorable number attached to them:

$$c_L=c_R=\frac{3\ell}{2G}.$$

Here \(\ell\) is the AdS radius and \(G\) is the three-dimensional Newton constant, with \(\hbar=1\). The central extension already arises in the classical charge algebra. It is not something that must first wait for a quantum anomaly.

## A clue, not a completed dictionary

If you know two-dimensional conformal field theory, “two Virasoro algebras” is a very familiar sound. It suggests left- and right-moving conformal symmetry. But hearing the symmetry is not the same as identifying the theory.

An analogy is recognizing the rules of chess without knowing the position on the board. The rules constrain every legal move. They do not tell you which pieces are present, how the game arrived here, or which legal position you are looking at. Similarly, a symmetry algebra does not specify the full spectrum and operator products of a CFT.

This distinction makes the Brown–Henneaux result more interesting, not less. It supplies a powerful piece of a future boundary description without pretending to supply every piece. It is a clue precise enough to calculate with.

Years later, the central charge would enter Strominger’s use of CFT state-counting asymptotics to reproduce black-hole entropy.[2] We will take that step after meeting the black hole. For the moment, notice the shape of the argument: geometry fixes a symmetry datum, and that datum will help constrain a huge number of states.

## The fine print is the plot

Different boundary conditions can define different physical problems. We should therefore avoid saying that every version of AdS₃ gravity automatically has exactly this boundary phase space. The celebrated result comes with a choice, and the choice is doing work.

This becomes a recurring habit in the series. Whenever someone says “the theory of three-dimensional gravity,” ask what they allow at infinity. A beautiful answer to one boundary-value problem need not answer another.

We started with a theory that seemed to have too few degrees of freedom. Now its boundary knows an infinite-dimensional algebra. Next comes another surprise: its bulk equations can be reorganized in the language of gauge theory.

title: When gravity became a gauge theory
deck: A change of variables opens a new toolbox—and makes the meaning of “the same theory” unexpectedly delicate.
text:
There are discoveries that add a new ingredient to a theory. There are others that reveal that the ingredients already on the table can be assembled into something you recognize. The Chern–Simons description of three-dimensional gravity belongs to the second kind.

Start with the familiar geometric language, but unpack the metric. A frame field \(e\) tells you how local measuring rods fit into spacetime. A spin connection \(\omega\) tells you how local frames rotate as you move. In first-order gravity, these are the variables you work with.

For Lorentzian AdS₃ gravity, put them together like this:

$$A=\omega+\frac{e}{\ell},\qquad \bar A=\omega-\frac{e}{\ell}.$$

Two combinations, with just a sign between them. Suddenly, the variables look like two gauge connections.

## The equation that changes the conversation

With a standard normalization of the Lie-algebra trace, the bulk Einstein action becomes a difference of Chern–Simons actions:

$$I_{\mathrm{grav}}=I_{\mathrm{CS}}[A]-I_{\mathrm{CS}}[\bar A],\qquad k_{\mathrm{CS}}=\frac{\ell}{4G}.$$

Appropriate boundary terms still have to be supplied. The relevant Lie algebra is \(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb R)\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb R)\). The two flatness equations encode constant curvature and vanishing torsion in the invertible-frame sector.

Achúcarro and Townsend gave the AdS supergravity construction in 1986.[1] Witten’s 1988 work developed the relation into a broad program for understanding and quantizing 2+1-dimensional gravity.[2] These are related landmarks, not interchangeable credits for a single paper.

Why is the rewriting exciting? Because it changes which questions are convenient to ask. A connection invites you to study parallel transport around loops. Flatness says small contractible loops are locally uninteresting, while noncontractible loops can retain holonomy. The global information that survived the disappearance of gravitational waves now has a natural mathematical language.

## A beautiful shortcut with a border crossing

It would be wonderful if the next sentence were simply: “Chern–Simons theory is understood, so quantum gravity is solved.” But that sentence silently crosses a border.

The identity between classical actions does not automatically identify the domains of the quantum path integrals. A pair of gauge connections can produce a degenerate frame through their difference. Such a frame does not define an ordinary invertible spacetime metric. Do we include it? If not, is our restriction preserved by the transformations we intend to quotient out?

There are other choices too. A Lie algebra does not fix the global gauge group. Allowed bundles, large transformations, boundary conditions, and the integration contour all affect the quantum problem. Writing the same local expression in two sets of variables does not answer those questions for us.

Imagine two maps with the same street pattern. Before using one to navigate the other, you still need to know whether the roads connect across the edge of the map, whether a bridge is open, and which apparent intersections are actually overpasses. Local agreement is a powerful start. Global instructions complete the route.

## A clue that keeps returning

The lasting gift of the CS reformulation is a language: connections, holonomies, moduli spaces, boundary states, and gluing. Later approaches can use that language while being more selective about the quantum construction.

The Virasoro TQFT proposal we will reach at the end explicitly distinguishes itself from ordinary \(SL(2,\mathbb R)\) Chern–Simons theory.[3] That distinction is part of the inheritance of the early observation, not a reason to forget it.

For the next chapter, keep one lesson close: a locally simple connection can carry important global information. In 1992, a particularly dramatic piece of global information entered the story. It had an event horizon.

refs: Bañados, Teitelboim & Zanelli (1992), The Black Hole in Three Dimensional Space Time
Bañados, Henneaux, Teitelboim & Zanelli (1993), Geometry of the 2+1 Black Hole
Strominger (1997/1998), Black Hole Entropy from Near-Horizon Microstates
title: The black hole that was still there
deck: No gravitational waves. Constant local curvature. And yet, an event horizon.
text:
Here is a wonderfully unreliable argument: three-dimensional gravity has no local gravitational waves; therefore it probably has no interesting black holes.

The first half is true for vacuum Einstein gravity. The second half does not follow. A black hole is defined by causal access to the outside world, not by the presence of a propagating graviton. The distinction becomes impossible to ignore in the solution introduced by Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli in 1992.[1]

The BTZ black hole lives in a theory with negative cosmological constant. For the uncharged solution we discuss here, every smooth local patch is still AdS₃. The black hole is in how the geometry is assembled globally.[2]

## Your neighborhood is innocent

Suppose you carried a tiny curvature laboratory across the horizon. In the idealized classical solution, it would not suddenly announce that the local curvature had become a new species of curvature. That is not how this horizon works.

The analogy with a cylinder returns, but now with causal structure at stake. Identifying points in a spacetime can change which paths are globally possible. Local measurements and global escape questions ask different things. A horizon belongs to the second category.

For a nonrotating BTZ black hole, one useful form of the metric is

$$ds^2=-\frac{r^2-r_+^2}{\ell^2}dt^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r^2-r_+^2}dr^2+r^2d\phi^2,\qquad \phi\sim\phi+2\pi.$$

The horizon sits at \(r=r_+\). The vanishing coefficient of \(dt^2\) and divergent radial coefficient there are features of these coordinates, not a divergent curvature invariant. The periodic identification of \(\phi\), meanwhile, is not decorative notation. It is part of the global specification.

## A small black hole with a large demand

A black hole brings thermodynamics into the room. In units with \(\hbar=k_B=1\), the nonrotating solution has

$$T=\frac{r_+}{2\pi\ell^2},\qquad S_{\mathrm{BH}}=\frac{2\pi r_+}{4G}.$$

The “area” in the entropy law is now the circumference of a circle. The dimension changed; the demand for an explanation did not. What microscopic states are being counted?

This is where “no local gravitons” becomes a productive provocation rather than a shortcut. If the entropy is large, then a quantum description must account for many states, even though the classical bulk lacks the familiar local waves. The challenge is to explain what the theory actually counts.

There is a useful restraint here. Finding a classical family of black holes does not tell us the exact quantum spectrum. Classical mass parameters can vary continuously; a particular quantum boundary theory may have a discrete spectrum. Moving between those descriptions requires an argument, not just a change of vocabulary.

## The two clues finally meet

At this point in our reading route, we have two pieces that seem made for one another. Brown–Henneaux gives a boundary symmetry with a central charge. BTZ gives a macroscopic entropy. Two-dimensional CFT has a way to connect symmetry data with high-energy state counting.

Strominger would use that connection to reproduce the black-hole entropy in the appropriate asymptotic regime.[3] The next article explains why that agreement is so striking—and why it still does not hand us the name and address of a complete boundary theory.

The surprise of BTZ is therefore more than “a black hole exists.” It turns a seemingly sparse theory into a sharp accounting problem. We removed local waves and somehow kept a very large bill.

Strominger (1997/1998), Black Hole Entropy from Near-Horizon Microstates

title: Counting states you have not met
deck: How symmetry gets the black-hole entropy right before we know the full microscopic story.
text:
Imagine being able to estimate the population of a city without meeting its residents. You would need unusually powerful constraints. In two-dimensional conformal field theory, modular invariance supplies something close to that power: it relates a thermal regime dominated by low-energy states to another that samples high-energy ones.

Cardy’s formula turns this relation into an asymptotic count.[1] It is not a census of individual states. It is a statement about how rapidly their number grows under suitable assumptions.

For a black hole, that can be exactly the question we need.

## The arithmetic is almost suspiciously good

Let \(h\) and \(\bar h\) denote the plane conformal weights, and let \(c_L=c_R=c\). Write the dimensionless left- and right-moving cylinder energies, including the vacuum Casimir shift, as \(E_L=h-c/24\) and \(E_R=\bar h-c/24\). In the regime where the Cardy estimate applies, the leading entropy takes the form

$$S\simeq2\pi\sqrt{\frac{cE_L}{6}}+2\pi\sqrt{\frac{cE_R}{6}}.$$

For BTZ, \(E_L=(\ell M+J)/2\) and \(E_R=(\ell M-J)/2\). Combine these with the Brown–Henneaux value \(c=3\ell/(2G)\), and the leading result becomes the horizon circumference divided by \(4G\). Strominger’s 1997/1998 argument made this agreement a central piece of the story.[2]

No arbitrary numerical adjustment is needed to rescue the coefficient. Geometry, boundary symmetry, and CFT asymptotics line up.

## What the success tells us

The agreement says that a suitable boundary CFT description has the right asymptotic capacity to account for the black-hole entropy. That is a substantial achievement. It connects a gravitational thermodynamic quantity to a microscopic counting framework.

But universal formulas are universal precisely because many different systems share them. A correct leading count need not single out one spectrum, much less one operator algebra. Two cities can have the same population and very different street plans.

There is also a regime question. At fixed central charge, Cardy is a high-energy asymptotic statement. Extending its usefulness into a large-central-charge gravitational regime requires control of the light spectrum; the work of Hartman, Keller, and Stoica makes the role of sparsity precise.[4] It would be careless to apply the expression indiscriminately to every black hole arbitrarily close to a threshold.

## Holography makes the question sharper

Maldacena’s AdS/CFT proposal supplied a much broader setting in which boundary quantum theories describe bulk gravity.[3] String-theoretic examples can come with explicit microscopic constructions and additional fields. They make holography concrete, but they do not automatically settle the separate problem of pure three-dimensional Einstein gravity.

“Find some AdS₃ quantum gravity with a CFT dual” and “identify the exact dual of a chosen pure-gravity theory” are different assignments. The second asks for a particularly austere bulk content while retaining consistency at every energy and in every observable.

We can now see why the subject remains lively after the entropy calculation. The leading number is right. The complete object that produces the number remains a more demanding target.

One way forward is to turn austerity into a rule: keep the states forced by boundary gravity, postpone other states as long as consistency permits, and see whether a CFT can survive. That is the temptation behind the extremal proposal. It is a much sharper question than “what might the boundary be?”—and a sharper question has more ways to fail.

refs: Frenkel, Lepowsky & Meurman (1988), Vertex Operator Algebras and the Monster
Gaiotto & Yin (2007), Genus Two Partition Functions of Extremal Conformal Field Theories
title: How empty can a quantum theory be?
deck: Pure gravity suggests a sparse spectrum. Extremal CFT asks how far that ambition can be pushed.
text:
Suppose you want a quantum theory of gravity with no extra matter. What does “no extra matter” look like from the boundary?

It cannot mean “no states.” We already have boundary excitations and black holes. The more interesting thought is to leave the low-energy spectrum as empty as possible, apart from the states that gravity itself seems to require.

This turns minimalism into a mathematical challenge. How much emptiness will consistency tolerate?

## The states you cannot remove

The vacuum of a two-dimensional CFT does not sit alone. Virasoro generators produce descendants: states organized by the symmetry algebra. For the gravitational interpretation, these vacuum descendants are the boundary-graviton sector.

A new primary is different. It is not obtained merely by acting on the vacuum with those generators. If we are trying to avoid additional light bulk particles, delaying such primaries is a natural idea.

Witten’s 2007 proposal explored this logic with a strong additional assumption: holomorphic factorization. In the chiral extremal problem, the central charge is \(c=24k\), with positive integer \(k\), and no non-vacuum primary appears through weight \(k\).[1] The first possible new primaries occur at weight \(k+1\).

This is a special ansatz for the boundary theory, not a consequence that follows from every possible definition of Einstein gravity.

## A partition function with very little freedom

The opening of the chiral partition function is fixed by the vacuum descendants:

$$Z(\tau)=q^{-k}\prod_{n=2}^{\infty}(1-q^n)^{-1}+O(q),\qquad q=e^{2\pi i\tau}.$$

Read the formula as a constraint on the expansion through the constant term. The product starts at two because the level-one vacuum descendant is absent. Modular invariance then severely restricts how this beginning can be completed.

The attraction is immediate: instead of searching blindly through all CFTs, we can write down sharply constrained candidate partition functions. At \(c=24\), the Monster CFT is an actual constructed theory, not merely a plausible series of coefficients.[2] It makes the proposal feel tantalizingly tangible.

## A guest list is not a party

But a partition function mostly tells us how many states of each energy are invited. It does not tell us how they interact.

A CFT needs operator products, consistency under different ways of combining operators, and amplitudes that fit together on different surfaces. Nonnegative integer degeneracies are necessary for a conventional discrete Hilbert-space interpretation. They do not construct those additional structures.

This is the trap of an especially elegant candidate. When modularity leaves almost no freedom, the resulting formula can look inevitable. Yet uniqueness of an answer to one restricted consistency problem is not existence of a solution to the full problem.

Higher-genus work soon pursued additional tests of extremal candidates.[3] We will return to what those tests do—and do not—establish. For now, keep the distinction between “a candidate partition function” and “a constructed CFT” in view.

## Two ways to search

The extremal route begins on the boundary: demand a sparse spectrum and see what survives. Another route begins in the bulk: sum the geometries that seem to belong in a gravitational path integral, and ask what spectrum the answer implies.

The two routes aim at related territory without making identical assumptions. In particular, the usual nonholomorphic gravitational saddle sum is not simply the extremal holomorphic ansatz in disguise.

The next article takes the bulk route. The striking result will be that a sum can be beautiful, computable, and symmetric—and still fail to look like the partition function of the quantum theory we wanted.

refs: Maloney & Witten (2007/2010), Quantum Gravity Partition Functions in Three Dimensions
Giombi, Maloney & Yin (2008), One-loop Partition Functions of 3D Gravity
Keller & Maloney (2014), Poincaré Series, 3D Gravity and CFT Spectroscopy
title: Add up the geometries. Do you get a theory?
deck: A gravitational path integral passes a symmetry test and runs into a state-counting problem.
text:
A Euclidean path integral offers an appealing instruction: hold the boundary fixed, fill it in every allowed way, and add the answers.

For a torus boundary, the instruction almost sounds manageable. A torus has two basic cycles. A solid-torus filling can make one of them contractible in the interior. Changing which cycle shrinks changes the bulk interpretation. Thermal AdS and Euclidean black-hole geometries enter the same conversation.

At last, perhaps the simplicity of three dimensions will pay the entire bill.

## The boundary keeps the score

The torus has a complex shape parameter \(\tau\). Different choices of its basic cycles are related by modular transformations. A sensible boundary partition function must behave consistently under those changes of description.

One can therefore begin with the thermal-AdS contribution and organize other fillings as modular images. The vacuum descendants we met earlier appear in the seed. At one loop, the relevant factor includes

$$\prod_{n=2}^{\infty}|1-q^n|^{-2}.$$

Giombi, Maloney, and Yin developed heat-kernel methods for these one-loop gravitational partition functions.[2] The result has a satisfying boundary interpretation: precisely the sort of vacuum-descendant tower we expected.

There is a catch before we even ask about states. The sum over images needs a regularization. “Sum all the fillings” is not a complete definition until we explain how that sum is made meaningful.

## Symmetry is a demanding friend, but not the only one

Maloney and Witten evaluated the regulated sum of the known saddle contributions and found that the resulting answer did not have the desired physical interpretation.[1] In particular, the spectrum inferred from this prescription was not that of an ordinary compact, unitary CFT with a discrete set of states and acceptable degeneracies.

This is a useful moment to pause. The problem is not that the expression looks ugly. It can satisfy an important symmetry requirement while failing other requirements of a quantum theory.

For a conventional discrete spectrum, a thermal trace is a sum over actual states. At each energy, the multiplicity counts something. A negative multiplicity cannot be repaired by admiring modular invariance. And a continuous spectral density needs a different physical interpretation from the discrete compact-CFT target.

Keller and Maloney’s later analysis of Poincaré series sharpens the interplay between modular completions and spectral data.[3] It also helps make clear why specifying a low-energy beginning and demanding modularity need not settle every ambiguity.

## What failed, exactly?

There is a bad way to retell this episode: “People calculated quantum gravity and proved it does not exist.” That conclusion is much broader than the calculation.

The result tests a prescription: a class of contributions, their weights and corrections, and a way of regularizing their sum. If it misses the intended answer, possibilities include missing contributions, an inadequate prescription, or an incorrect expectation about the target. Distinguishing those possibilities is research, not a footnote.

Imagine assembling a machine from every part listed on a diagram. It does not run. You have learned something decisive about that assembly. You have not yet established that no machine performing the task can exist.

## A failure worth keeping

The calculation raises the standard for every future proposal. A credible construction must do more than reproduce a classical saddle or a leading entropy. It must explain how the complete answer becomes a legitimate quantum object.

And even a perfect torus partition function would not finish the job. A spectrum tells us who is present. To learn how the states interact, we need to ask the theory a more elaborate question. The simplest next move is to give the boundary another handle.

refs: Gaiotto & Yin (2007), Genus Two Partition Functions of Extremal Conformal Field Theories
Yin (2007), Partition Functions of Three-Dimensional Pure Gravity
Gaberdiel, Keller & Volpato (2010), Genus Two Partition Functions of Chiral Conformal Field Theories
title: A second handle asks harder questions
deck: A spectrum is a beginning. Sewing surfaces asks whether the pieces know how to work together.
text:
A torus partition function is an extraordinarily informative answer to a rather specific question. It tells us about a trace over states. It does not, by itself, hand us every interaction coefficient of the theory.

That is why adding a second handle is more than a request for a prettier picture. A genus-two surface can be assembled by gluing simpler pieces, and the gluing brings additional CFT data into play.

If the torus is an inventory, sewing asks whether the inventory can be put to work.

## Cut, insert, join

Picture cutting a surface along a circle. To glue the two sides back together, a quantum theory inserts a complete set of intermediate states and sums over them. A long thin tube makes this especially intuitive: low-energy states dominate propagation along it.

Now use pieces with three circular boundaries, often called pairs of pants. The name is homely; the information is not. Their amplitudes are related to three-point data. Gluing many such pieces involves both the spectrum and the rules for combining operators.

There is more than one way to cut the same surface. A genuine theory must give compatible answers. A change of sewing channel cannot change the physical object merely because we used a different assembly manual.

This is the broader reason higher-genus amplitudes matter. They bring geometry, factorization limits, and operator products into one consistency problem.

## The extremal test bench

In 2007, Gaiotto and Yin constructed genus-two partition functions for particular extremal-CFT candidates and studied stringent consistency tests.[1] Yin also investigated gravitational partition functions and their relation to these boundary constructions, including handlebody contributions.[2]

The bulk picture has a satisfying counterpart to sewing. A boundary Riemann surface can admit different fillings; in a handlebody filling, selected boundary cycles become contractible. Once again, knowing the boundary shape does not uniquely tell us which bulk geometry to choose.

But this episode comes with an important correction to an overly triumphant retelling. Gaberdiel, Keller, and Volpato showed that consistent genus-two vacuum amplitudes for the proposed extremal theories can exist for all \(k\), while not testing their consistency beyond what is already testable at genus one in that setting.[3]

So “higher genus probes more structure in general” must not be turned into “this particular genus-two success proves the extremal theories exist.” The actual strength of a test depends on the data and constraints that enter it.

## More checks are not automatically independent checks

This is a lesson that travels well outside gravity. Suppose a calculation passes ten tests, but nine are mathematical consequences of the first. You have excellent evidence that you implemented the first condition consistently. You do not have ten independent reasons to believe the entire theory exists.

The useful question is not how complicated a check looks. It is which new failure it could have detected.

For a proposed boundary dual, a convincing program therefore needs to keep track of exactly what has been constructed: a modular function, a collection of amplitudes, consistent operator products, or an actual theory satisfying the full requirements. These achievements are related, but the labels should not be silently exchanged.

## One boundary, several holes; several boundaries, another puzzle

So far we have made one boundary surface more complicated. Another possibility is to ask for multiple disconnected boundaries. In the bulk, connected geometries may join them.

That shift changes the question dramatically. Instead of asking how one theory sews its amplitudes, we confront whether a connected gravitational contribution is compatible with the factorization expected from a fixed boundary theory. The next article follows that tension into the language of ensembles.

refs: Cotler & Jensen (2020/2021), AdS3 Gravity and Random CFT
Chandra, Collier, Hartman & Maloney (2022), Semiclassical 3D Gravity as an Average of Large-c CFTs
Maloney & Witten (2020), Averaging over Narain Moduli Space
title: One theory—or many?
deck: Wormholes invite a statistical interpretation. The hard part is specifying exactly what is random.
text:
Take a fixed quantum theory and evaluate its partition function on two disconnected boundary components. With independent copies and no extra coupling, the answer factorizes. That is the ordinary expectation.

Now look at a gravitational path integral. It may include connected geometries joining those boundaries. A wormhole contribution seems to know about both components at once.

What, then, is the boundary quantity that gravity is computing?

## Statistics offers a natural sentence

For random variables, the average of a product need not equal the product of the averages. Their difference is a connected correlation. Schematically,

$$\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle-\langle Z_1\rangle\langle Z_2\rangle$$

can be nonzero even when each individual member of the ensemble defines an ordinary factorizing theory. The same random choice of theory enters both factors.

This gives wormholes a plausible statistical vocabulary. A connected bulk contribution might encode a connected correlation of boundary data rather than a failure of quantum mechanics inside a single boundary theory.

The word “might” is doing necessary work. A suggestive structure is the start of an interpretation, not its complete definition.

## Calculations that make the idea concrete

Cotler and Jensen computed an AdS₃ gravitational path integral on the topology of a torus times an interval and extracted spectral correlations, including near-threshold behavior suggestive of random-matrix structure.[1] Their torus-wormhole calculation should not be casually described as an ordinary smooth real Einstein saddle; off-shell aspects of the gravitational prescription matter.

Chandra, Collier, Hartman, and Maloney subsequently developed an ensemble of large-central-charge CFT data, constrained by bootstrap information, which reproduces a variety of semiclassical gravitational results.[2] This extends the statistical picture beyond a loose analogy.

There are also settings where an averaging measure is supplied explicitly. Narain CFTs provide one such laboratory.[3] But the existence of a well-defined average in that family does not automatically supply the measure needed for pure Einstein gravity. The theories and the bulk constructions are different.

## “An ensemble” of what?

The phrase can conceal several targets. We might be averaging exact, complete CFTs. We might have a statistical model of selected operator dimensions and OPE coefficients. We might only reproduce a particular family of observables in a controlled asymptotic regime.

These are all potentially useful. They are not the same claim.

To see the difference, imagine receiving a table of proposed means and correlations for several random quantities. Before declaring that a probability distribution exists, you must check that those numbers can be moments of one positive measure. A covariance matrix, for example, cannot have a negative quadratic form on an allowed test vector. Passing that test still does not settle every higher-moment requirement.

For CFTs the challenge is richer, because each sample is supposed to satisfy its own consistency conditions. Randomly selecting plausible dimensions and coefficients does not automatically produce crossing symmetry, unitarity, or a complete theory.

## The question became more precise

The statistical perspective does not make the search for a boundary definition disappear. It tells us to specify a different possible object with equal care. What is sampled? Which observables are matched? At what precision? What is exact, and what is a large-\(c\) approximation?

That is progress even before the ultimate measure is in hand. We have replaced a slogan with a set of tests.

One difficulty remains especially practical: how do we compute sufficiently rich bulk amplitudes to test these ideas? A modern answer returns to the old themes of topology, boundary states, and gluing—but with Virasoro conformal blocks at the center of the machinery.

title: A new machine for an old question
deck: Virasoro TQFT turns gluing into a computational language. A full definition of gravity still asks for more.
text:
By now the same verbs keep returning: cut, fill, glue, transform, sum. We have used them for gauge connections, boundary surfaces, CFT states, and gravitational geometries. It is reasonable to ask whether a single mathematical machine can organize more of this work.

Virasoro TQFT is a modern proposal for such a machine. Its appeal is not simply that it says “gravity is topological.” That phrase was never enough to tell us what to calculate. The appeal is a much more concrete set of ingredients and operations.

## Building blocks that know how to change channels

A conformal block isolates a particular symmetry-organized contribution to a CFT correlator or amplitude. It knows about an intermediate representation and the descendants attached to it. Different decompositions of a surface lead to different block bases.

Moving between those bases requires transformation kernels. These are not arbitrary changes of notation: their identities ensure compatibility among different ways of decomposing and reassembling a surface.

Work on Liouville theory, noncompact quantum groups, and quantum Teichmüller theory developed deep connections among these structures.[2][3] This is an important strand of the history that our short route only touches. The 2023 gravity proposal did not summon its mathematical ingredients from nowhere.

## From identities to three-manifolds

In a topological quantum field theory, surfaces carry state spaces and three-dimensional cobordisms define operations on them. Gluing geometries corresponds to composing the associated operations. The promise is that a difficult-looking manifold can be handled by cutting it into tractable pieces, provided the rules are consistent.

Collier, Eberhardt, and Zhang proposed a precise AdS₃-gravity reformulation using a TQFT based on Teichmüller-space quantization and Virasoro data.[1] Their construction provides a systematic method for fixed-topology gravitational calculations, with nontrivial mapping-class-group considerations in relating the TQFT to gravity.

This is not an ordinary finite-state topological theory, and the paper explicitly distinguishes it from standard \(SL(2,\mathbb R)\) Chern–Simons theory. The resemblance to the early CS story is real; replacing one name with the other would lose the point.

## What “solving” can mean

There is a substantial difference between an algorithm for an amplitude at a chosen topology and a complete prescription for the full gravitational path integral.

Once an amplitude is available, we can still ask which topologies to include, how to weight them, whether the resulting sum converges or needs a prescription, and how off-shell contributions fit into the definition. We can also ask what exact boundary object reproduces the complete answer.

These questions are not complaints about a useful machine. A machine can solve an important class of calculations while leaving the choice of what to calculate open. Conflating the two would make it harder to appreciate the actual achievement.

Think of obtaining a powerful grammar for assembling sentences. The grammar is a real advance. It does not by itself decide which book to write, how to sum over every possible book, or whether that sum defines the object you intended.

## The route comes back to its beginning

Our first article asked what survives when local gravitational waves disappear. We now have a much richer answer: global geometry, boundary symmetry, black-hole states, operator consistency, and the problem of a complete quantum definition.

The CS observation taught us to reorganize the variables. BTZ forced us to count states. Modular sums taught us that symmetry alone does not guarantee a sensible spectrum. Higher genus sharpened the meaning of consistency. Wormholes widened the possible boundary target. Virasoro TQFT supplies new ways to compute the objects that these questions demand.

This selected route ends with a method and a question, rather than a claim that the subject is finished. Given all this structure, what precisely is the quantum object whose amplitudes we are calculating?

That question is the reason to keep the notebook open.
